title: Intercalation and the Runaway Cell
topic: lithium ion batteries and thermal runaway
paragraphs: In a teardown lab the steel can of a spent cylindrical cell is cut away, and almost nothing inside looks like a source of power.

What comes out is a tight spiral of foil that unrolls into a strip about a meter long and as wide as a finger, two coated metal ribbons with a sheet of white plastic thinner than a hair between them, everything damp with a clear organic liquid.
Every rechargeable battery that came before worked by taking metal apart and putting it back together.
In a lead acid cell the active material on both plates turns to lead sulfate on discharge and back again on charge, and a nickel cadmium cell does much the same with cadmium.
The first rechargeable lithium cells pushed the idea to its limit, using a sheet of lithium metal itself, the lightest metal there is, as the negative electrode.
Plating is an untidy process.

Metal does not return as a smooth even layer; it builds up preferentially wherever the surface already bulges, because a bump concentrates the electric field around it, and each cycle leaves the surface rougher than the last.
With lithium the roughness takes the form of whiskers and mossy growths called dendrites, which creep outward like frost across a window.
Some snap off and are lost.
Others keep going until they touch the opposite electrode, shorting a sealed can of lithium metal and flammable solvent.
Cells of that design were withdrawn from sale.
The idea that rescued the technology was to stop making and unmaking metal altogether.
In an intercalation electrode lithium is never reduced to metal at all.
It arrives as an ion, slots into a gap already waiting inside a crystal, and later leaves the same way.
The crystal is called a host, which here does not mean anything living but a rigid framework that takes in guest ions between its layers and gives them back without being consumed.
Graphite is the standard host on the negative side, its carbon sheets stacked like the pages of a closed book, and a layered metal oxide is the host on the positive side.
The cell runs by rocking lithium from one host to the other and back.
The numbers are worth holding onto.

A fully charged graphite electrode holds one lithium for every six carbon atoms, and that much lithium swells the graphite by roughly a tenth of its volume, a strain the stacked sheets absorb without coming apart.
A common positive electrode is a layered oxide of nickel, manganese, and cobalt.
Another is lithium iron phosphate.
A cell built from graphite and a layered oxide rests near 3.7 volts and is charged to about 4.2.
The powders are spread onto foils only tens of micrometers thick: copper on the negative side, which resists attack at low voltage, and aluminum on the positive side, which survives high voltage.
None of this settles what the lithium travels through.
Water is out of the question.

Every solvent has a voltage window, the span between the voltage at which it begins to break down at one electrode and the voltage at which it breaks down at the other, and the window for water is a little over one volt wide.
A lithium ion cell runs at nearly four.
So the electrolyte is a lithium salt, usually lithium hexafluorophosphate, dissolved in a blend of organic carbonate solvents.
Those solvents carry ions well and tolerate high voltage.
They are also flammable, with flash points at or below room temperature.
A carbonate electrolyte should not survive contact with charged graphite either, and strictly speaking it does not.
During the first charge, performed at the factory under controlled conditions, a thin skin of decomposition products builds up on the graphite surface.
This layer, the solid electrolyte interphase, is the quiet hero of the design: it conducts lithium ions but not electrons, so once it covers the surface the reaction that built it shuts itself off.
Forming it permanently locks away a few percent of the cell's lithium.
The layer is nanometers thick, chemically fragile, and the first thing to give way when a cell gets hot.
The white film is the separator, and its two jobs pull against each other.
Mechanically it must keep the electrodes apart.
Chemically it must not obstruct the ions.
So it is a porous polyolefin membrane, typically ten to twenty five micrometers thick and about forty percent empty space by volume, with pores well under a micrometer across.

Many are built as three bonded layers, polypropylene outside and polyethylene in the middle, so that the polyethylene melts near 130 degrees Celsius and its pores close, choking off ion flow, while the higher melting polypropylene holds the sheet together for another thirty degrees.
Intercalation was supposed to retire dendrites, and in ordinary use it does.
But intercalation has a speed limit.

Ions must not only reach the graphite surface, they must work their way into it, and that is slow when the cell is cold, slow when the charging current is high, and slow when the graphite is already nearly full.
If ions arrive faster than the graphite can take them in, they accept an electron at the surface instead and plate out as lithium metal after all.
Given enough of those mossy deposits, some will reach across.
A stray metal particle left in during manufacturing can short a cell unaided.
What follows is a sequence that is by now well characterized.
Somewhere between roughly 80 and 120 degrees Celsius the solid electrolyte interphase begins to break down, exposing charged graphite to liquid electrolyte and giving off heat.
That heat drives the next step rather than waiting for it.
Near 130 degrees the separator's shutdown layer closes its pores, which helps only if the cell can now cool faster than it is warming.
If it cannot, the separator itself melts and shrinks back from the edges above about 160 degrees, and the electrodes meet across an area far larger than any dendrite could bridge.
The internal short dumps the cell's stored charge as heat in seconds.
Above roughly 200 degrees the positive electrode starts to come apart, and a layered oxide that comes apart gives off oxygen.
That detail separates a battery fire from an ordinary solvent fire.
The cell now holds fuel, an oxidizer, and a heat source inside one sealed steel can, and no longer needs the room's air in order to burn.

Pressure climbs until a scored disc in the can lets go, and the cell vents a jet of hot gas that is itself flammable: hydrogen, carbon monoxide, small hydrocarbons, and vaporized solvent, with hydrogen fluoride from the fluorine bearing salt.
Crews flood such fires mainly to cool the neighboring cells.
The word runaway is doing precise work there.
Heat production inside the cell climbs steeply with temperature, while the cell's ability to shed heat into its surroundings grows only in proportion to how much hotter it is than the room.
Below a certain temperature removal wins and a warm cell cools off.
Above it production wins, every degree of warming buys further warming, and nothing done from outside can reach the reaction.
It is tempting to read that cascade as a malfunction, and popular coverage usually does.
The framing is misleading.
Every step is the same chemistry the cell performs on purpose, running with nothing left to hold it back.

A charged cell is by design a metastable arrangement, a strong reducing agent and a strong oxidizing agent parked tens of micrometers apart and kept from reacting by a plastic film and a few nanometers of surface chemistry.
That separation is the entire safety strategy.
Engineers do not claim to have removed the hazard.
They claim something more modest, that they have made its onset rare and its spread slow.
This is also why the familiar complaint, that these cells are dangerous because they store so much energy, is only half right.

A good lithium ion cell holds something like 250 to 300 watt hours per kilogram, seven or eight times what a lead acid battery of the same mass holds, and that figure is why the technology displaced everything else.

The stored electrical energy is not even the largest term: when a cell burns, the combustion of its electrolyte and electrode materials releases several times more energy than the charge it was holding.
Density and severity are two readings of a single property.
One response is to pick a less energetic chemistry.

Lithium iron phosphate binds its oxygen inside phosphate groups, far more tightly than a layered oxide does, so the positive electrode does not readily give up oxygen and the onset of runaway sits at a markedly higher temperature.
Such cells are genuinely harder to set off.
They also sit at a lower voltage and store meaningfully less energy for their mass, which in a vehicle means either a shorter range or a heavier pack.
The safer chemistry is not simply the better one.
Most of the remaining work happens at the pack, where the compromises are easiest to see.
A management system watches each group of cells and refuses to charge a cold one quickly, because cold and fast is exactly when plating begins.

Cells are spaced apart, wrapped in mats that swell and insulate when heated, and seated on cooling plates, and vents are aimed so that hot gas leaves through the floor of a vehicle rather than into the cabin.
Each of those measures costs volume and mass that could have carried more cells, so every firebreak is paid for out of the range the chemistry was chosen to deliver.
The newest packs bond cells directly into the structure and delete the module walls between them, buying back several percent of usable volume and removing a firebreak in the same stroke.
Designers accept that trade only when they can show, by setting one cell alight on a test bench, that its neighbors stay cool.
The goal is narrower than the public version of it: not a cell that cannot burn, but a pack in which one cell's bad day stays one cell's bad day.

questions.stem: According to the passage, taking lithium into graphite changes the graphite's volume in which way?
choices: It swells by roughly a tenth.
It shrinks by roughly a tenth.
It swells by about half.
It roughly doubles.
It stays exactly the same, which is the whole point of intercalation.

proof.quote: swells the graphite by roughly a tenth of its volume

questions.why: Paragraph 5 gives the figure outright: one lithium for every six carbons at full charge, and that much lithium swells the graphite by roughly a tenth of its volume.
distractorNotes: Right size, wrong direction. Lithium moving in swells the graphite rather than shrinking it.
Half is the wrong number. The passage says roughly a tenth, small enough for the stacked sheets to absorb.
Too extreme. Nothing in the passage describes a volume change anywhere near that large.
Intercalation does keep the framework intact, but the passage still reports a real swelling of about a tenth.

questions.stem: The passage says lead acid cells and nickel cadmium cells share which feature?
choices: They use a lithium salt dissolved in carbonate solvents.
They hold lithium ions between stacked carbon sheets.
They shut down when a plastic membrane melts near 130 degrees Celsius.
They depend on a thin surface layer that conducts ions but blocks electrons.
Their active material is broken down on discharge and rebuilt on charge.

proof.quote: taking metal apart and putting it back together
turns to lead sulfate on discharge and back again on charge

questions.why: Paragraph 2 groups the older chemistries by one habit. The electrode material is chemically taken apart as the cell discharges and put back together as it charges.
distractorNotes: A carbonate electrolyte belongs to the lithium ion cell described in paragraph 6.
That is intercalation, the later idea introduced in paragraph 4, not how these older cells work.
The melting membrane is the separator of a lithium ion cell in paragraph 8.
The surface layer is the solid electrolyte interphase of paragraph 7, part of the lithium ion design.

questions.stem: In the three layer separator the passage describes, the polyethylene layer is responsible for
choices: keeping the membrane about forty percent empty by volume
closing its pores near 130 degrees and choking off ion flow
raising the temperature at which the positive electrode gives off oxygen
carrying electrons between the two electrodes
holding the sheet together for about thirty degrees more

proof.quote: the polyethylene melts near 130 degrees Celsius and its pores close, choking off ion flow

questions.why: Paragraph 8 splits the two jobs. The polyethylene in the middle melts near 130 degrees Celsius so its pores close and ion flow stops, while the outer polypropylene keeps the sheet intact longer.
distractorNotes: Forty percent empty space describes the membrane as a whole, not something one layer contributes.
Oxygen release above roughly 200 degrees is a property of the positive electrode in paragraph 11, not of the separator.
A separator exists to keep the electrodes from touching, so carrying electrons between them is exactly what it prevents.
That is the polypropylene's role, which holds on for roughly another thirty degrees.

questions.stem: According to the passage, forming the solid electrolyte interphase costs the cell
choices: a few percent of its lithium, permanently
the ability to use a carbonate electrolyte after the first charge
roughly a tenth of its volume
about forty percent of its internal space
most of its capacity to take charge in the cold

proof.quote: permanently locks away a few percent of the cell's lithium

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the layer builds during the factory's first charge and that making it permanently locks away a few percent of the cell's lithium.
distractorNotes: The interphase is what lets the carbonate electrolyte keep working, so it does not retire it.
A tenth of the volume is graphite's swelling in paragraph 5, a different number in a different place.
Forty percent is the separator's empty space in paragraph 8.
Trouble charging in the cold comes from intercalation's speed limit in paragraph 9, not from forming this layer.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that once the separator melts and pulls back from the edges, what happens next is that
choices: a scored disc opens and the cell vents
the pores close and ion flow stops
charged graphite is exposed to liquid electrolyte for the very first time
the electrodes meet across a much larger area
the positive electrode begins giving off oxygen

proof.quote: the electrodes meet across an area far larger than any dendrite could bridge

questions.why: Paragraph 10 runs the steps in order. The shutdown layer closes near 130 degrees, and if the cell keeps warming the separator itself melts above about 160, letting the electrodes meet over an area no dendrite could match.
distractorNotes: Venting is driven by rising pressure in paragraph 11, after the internal short has already dumped the cell's charge.
That is the earlier step near 130 degrees, and it is the opposite effect.
Charged graphite meets electrolyte first, when the interphase breaks down between about 80 and 120 degrees.
Oxygen release comes later, above roughly 200 degrees, in paragraph 11.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 4, "host" most nearly means
choices: a large number of something
an organism that shelters another organism
a framework that holds ions without being consumed
a liquid in which a salt is dissolved
an electrode made of metal that gives up its electrons readily

proof.quote: a rigid framework that takes in guest ions
gives them back without being consumed

questions.why: Paragraph 4 defines the word on the spot: not anything living, but a rigid framework that takes in guest ions between its layers and gives them back without being used up.
distractorNotes: A real dictionary sense of the word, but the passage is naming a crystal, not a quantity.
The passage rules this sense out in the same sentence where it introduces the word.
That describes the carbonate solvent of paragraph 6, not the crystal.
That describes the lithium metal electrode of paragraph 2, which is exactly what intercalation replaced.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 6, "window" most nearly means
choices: a pore in the separator that ions pass through
the gap between two stacked sheets of carbon
the voltage range a solvent can survive
an opening in the steel can that relieves pressure
a short stretch of time in which something is possible

proof.quote: Every solvent has a voltage window
the span between the voltage at which it begins to break down

questions.why: Paragraph 6 builds the meaning as it uses the term: the span between the voltage where a solvent starts breaking down at one electrode and where it breaks down at the other. Water's span is a little over a volt and the cell needs nearly four.
distractorNotes: The separator's pores appear in paragraph 8 and are never called a window.
The space between carbon sheets is where lithium sits in paragraph 4.
That is the scored vent disc of paragraph 11.
The everyday sense of the word, but this paragraph is measuring volts rather than minutes.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that charging a cold cell at a high current is risky because
choices: the interphase thickens and locks away more of the cell's lithium
lithium plates onto the graphite instead of entering it
the separator's pores close before the cell is full
the electrolyte freezes and stops carrying ions
the positive electrode starts releasing oxygen at low temperature

proof.quote: plate out as lithium metal after all
cold and fast is exactly when plating begins

questions.why: Paragraph 9 supplies the mechanism. Working into graphite is slow when the cell is cold and slow when the current is high, and ions that arrive faster than the graphite can take them in accept an electron at the surface and plate out as metal.
distractorNotes: The interphase is built during the factory's first charge in paragraph 7, not during cold fast charging.
Pore closure is a heat triggered shutdown near 130 degrees, which is the opposite situation.
The passage never mentions the electrolyte freezing. The limit it describes is how fast lithium can work its way into graphite.
Oxygen release needs roughly 200 degrees, nowhere near a cold cell.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 13, a fully charged cell sitting idle on a shelf is best described as
choices: held apart from a reaction its own chemistry favors
already undergoing slow thermal runaway at room temperature
gradually consuming its separator with every passing day
chemically stable, since its reactants cannot reach one another
safe because its electrolyte will not burn

proof.quote: a metastable arrangement
kept from reacting by a plastic film

questions.why: Paragraph 13 calls a charged cell metastable: a strong reducing agent and a strong oxidizing agent kept from each other by a plastic film and a few nanometers of surface chemistry. Blocked is not the same as having no reason to react.
distractorNotes: Runaway in this passage is a rapid cascade above a crossing temperature, not something a room temperature cell is doing.
Nothing in the passage describes the separator wearing away during storage or ordinary use.
Metastable is the passage's own word, and it means the reaction is favored but blocked, not that there is nothing to block.
Paragraph 6 says plainly that the carbonate solvents are flammable.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
choices: Thermal runaway begins with the interphase and ends when the cell vents.
Lithium cells fail mainly because manufacturers economize on the separator film that keeps the electrodes apart.
Lithium iron phosphate should replace layered oxides everywhere they are now used.
Intercalation cured the plating problem, but the energy it unlocked is also what makes failure severe.
The separator is the only thing standing between a cell and a fire.

proof.quote: Intercalation was supposed to retire dendrites, and in ordinary use it does.
that figure is why the technology displaced everything else
Density and severity are two readings of a single property.

questions.why: The passage moves from why intercalation replaced plating to what a cell does when it overheats, then states the link in paragraph 14: density and severity are two readings of a single property.
distractorNotes: That is a fair summary of paragraphs 10 and 11 alone, not of the whole passage.
The passage argues the opposite, that the cascade is ordinary chemistry running unchecked rather than a cut corner.
Paragraph 15 calls the safer chemistry a different point on the same curve and names what it costs.
Too narrow and too absolute. The interphase, the management system, cell spacing and vent paths are all described as barriers too.

questions.stem: Paragraph 12 is included mainly in order to
choices: explain why the failure keeps going on its own
describe how a management system tracks cell temperature
show that reaction rates can be measured with precision
catalog the gases a venting cell releases
recommend lithium iron phosphate for vehicles

proof.quote: The word runaway is doing precise work there.
every degree of warming buys further warming

questions.why: Paragraph 12 sets heat produced against heat removed. Above a certain temperature production wins and every degree of warming buys further warming, which is what makes the word runaway accurate.
distractorNotes: Management systems appear in paragraph 16.
The temperature dependence is used to explain a feedback, not to make a point about measurement.
The gases are listed in paragraph 11.
No such recommendation is made, and paragraph 15 is careful to name what that chemistry costs.

questions.stem: How do the early paragraphs of the passage relate to the later ones?
choices: The early ones give the history and the later ones give a procedure the reader is meant to follow step by step.
The early ones build the cell part by part; the later ones follow those same parts failing.
The early ones describe one chemistry and the later ones describe a rival chemistry.
Both stretches make the same argument from two different sets of numbers.
The early ones raise a problem the later ones report as solved.

proof.quote: The cell runs by rocking lithium from one host to the other and back.
the solid electrolyte interphase begins to break down
the separator itself melts
the positive electrode starts to come apart

questions.why: The passage introduces the foils, the hosts, the electrolyte, the interphase and the separator in turn, then walks those same components through the heating sequence in paragraphs 10 and 11.
distractorNotes: There is history in paragraph 2, but the passage never hands the reader a procedure.
Lithium iron phosphate gets one paragraph near the end and is not what the later paragraphs are about.
The two stretches do different work, one descriptive and one causal.
Nothing is reported as solved. The passage closes on a compromise and a deliberately narrow goal.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the popular habit of calling thermal runaway a malfunction is best described as
choices: admiring of the clarity it brings
neutral, taking no position
corrective but not scornful
alarmed
dismissive of the concern itself

proof.quote: The framing is misleading.
Every step is the same chemistry the cell performs on purpose

questions.why: Paragraph 13 says the framing is misleading and then explains what is actually going on, calmly and without mocking anyone. That is a correction rather than an attack.
distractorNotes: Nothing in the paragraph praises the popular framing.
Calling a framing misleading is taking a position.
The paragraph is measured and explanatory rather than alarmed.
The author corrects how the hazard is described, not the idea that there is a hazard.

questions.stem: In reporting what engineers claim about the hazard, the author comes across as
choices: doubtful that any of the safety work accomplishes much
certain that the hazard has been engineered out of existence
indifferent to whether the claim turns out to hold
impatient with how slowly the field is moving
approving of a claim kept deliberately narrow

proof.quote: They claim something more modest
The goal is narrower than the public version of it

questions.why: Paragraph 13 calls the engineers' claim more modest and lets it stand: onset made rare, spread made slow. That word reads as approval of a claim that does not overreach.
distractorNotes: The passage treats those measures as real and effective within limits, not as empty.
The paragraph states directly that engineers do not claim to have removed the hazard.
Indifference would not single the claim out as modest, which is a favorable word here.
The passage says nothing at all about the pace of the work.

questions.stem: The passage describes all of the following as pack level measures EXCEPT
choices: mats that swell and insulate as they heat
aiming the vents so that hot gas leaves through the floor rather than the cabin
setting cells apart from one another
refusing to charge a cold pack quickly
flooding the pack with inert gas

proof.quote: Cells are spaced apart
wrapped in mats that swell and insulate when heated
hot gas leaves through the floor of a vehicle rather than into the cabin
refuses to charge a cold one quickly
Crews flood such fires mainly to cool the neighboring cells.

questions.why: Paragraph 16 lists spacing, swelling mats, cooling plates, aimed vents and a management system that limits cold fast charging. An inert gas flood never appears; the only flooding in the passage is water used to cool neighboring cells in paragraph 11.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 16 describes mats that swell and insulate when heated.
Paragraph 16 says vents are aimed so hot gas leaves through the floor of a vehicle.
Paragraph 16 lists cell spacing directly.
Paragraph 16 says the management system refuses to charge a cold cell quickly.

questions.stem: A reader who wanted to know why a lithium ion cell cannot use water as its electrolyte should look in
choices: paragraph 5
paragraph 11
paragraph 2
paragraph 6
paragraph 4

proof.quote: Water is out of the question.
the window for water is a little over one volt wide

questions.why: Paragraph 6 rules water out and gives the reason: water's voltage window is a little over one volt wide and the cell runs at nearly four.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 gives the cell's numbers, including its voltages, but not why water is unsuitable.
Paragraph 11 covers the positive electrode giving off oxygen and the cell venting.
Paragraph 2 covers the plating chemistries that came before lithium ion.
Paragraph 4 explains intercalation and what a host is.
